subtype: Approach: pairs a trigger with an action [Action]
passage: Francis lived in the school hostel, where the rule was that shoes go on the rack outside room six. Most evenings his shoes ended up under his bed, and Warden Rehana had reminded him three times that week. On Thursday, in the corridor, Francis told himself, "If my shoes are lying near the door when I come in from school, then they go on the rack." He said it twice, like a spell. That afternoon he dropped his bag, saw the shoes he had just kicked off, and put them on the rack without needing to think. Rehana walked past, glanced at the rack and smiled. "Good," said Rehana. Francis grinned. "The shoes told me."

qa.q: Where does the hostel rule say shoes go?
qa.a: The rule was that shoes go on the rack outside room six.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Rehana smiled at the rack?
qa.a: Francis felt proud and pleased, shown by the grin and the joke that the shoes told him.

qa.q: What could Francis do if he forgets the plan on a tired day?
qa.a: Francis could put a small picture of a shoe by the door as another cue, or ask Rehana to remind him for a few days.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about the change?
qa.a: Rehana might feel pleased and relieved not to have to remind Francis again.

grounding: Shows a boy linking a visible cue to an action so that seeing his shoes triggers putting them on the rack.

subtype: Approach: pairs a trigger with an action [Action]
passage:
I'm Dhruv, and Mridul is my neighbour. Every evening his mother used to shout, "Mridul, shoes!" because he kicked them off in the doorway and ran inside.
Last month something changed. I was at his house after school, and he took off his shoes in the doorway like always. But then he stopped, looked at them, and said to himself, "Shoes by the door, then rack." He picked them up and put them on the wooden rack.
I asked why he talked to his shoes. He said, "If I see them there, I put them away. That's the rule. Then I don't have to remember."
Now I notice it every day. He sees the shoes, and his hands just do it. His mother hasn't shouted about shoes all month. I don't know if he's proud, but he grins a little every time.

qa.q: What does Mridul say to himself by the door?
What might Mridul's little grin every time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels proud and pleased that the rule works, though Dhruv can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Mridul use the same kind of rule for?
qa.a: He could make a rule like "if I put my bag down, then I take out my lunch box," so another chore happens without having to remember.

qa.q: How is Mridul's mother affected by the new rule?
qa.a: She hasn't had to shout about shoes all month, so evenings are calmer for her.

grounding: It shows a boy pairing a trigger with an action: when he sees his shoes by the door after school, he puts them on the rack.

subtype: Approach: pairs a trigger with an action [Action]
passage:
Monday. Tenzin came home from school, dropped his shoes in the doorway, and his older sister Binita tripped over them carrying the laundry. "Every single day!" she said.
That night Tenzin lay in bed thinking. He always forgot because he was thinking about snacks, not shoes. So he needed something to remind him that wasn't his memory.
Tuesday. He made a rule and said it out loud at the door: "If I see my shoes on the floor, then they go on the rack." He put them there. It felt silly.
Wednesday. He came in, saw the shoes, and his hands moved before he thought about it. Rack.
Two weeks later, Binita came home and stopped. There were no shoes in the doorway at all. "Did Amma make you do this?"
"No," Tenzin said, eating his biscuit. "The shoes remind me."

qa.q: What did Binita trip over on Monday?
qa.a: She tripped over his shoes in the doorway.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when she found no shoes in the doorway?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and pleased, even a little suspicious, asking if Amma had made him do it.

qa.q: What else could Tenzin do if the rule stops working some days?
qa.a: He could put a small picture of shoes on the door as an extra reminder, so the trigger is easier to notice.

qa.q: How does the rule change things for Binita?
qa.a: Binita no longer trips over shoes while carrying laundry, so the doorway is safer and she is less annoyed.

grounding: It shows a boy linking a trigger to an action: when he sees his shoes on the floor after school, he puts them on the rack without effort.
